note: Explains how to calibrate controls to risk severity, and treats NIS2 and DORA as risk multipliers on the same system.
title: Risk, Reasonableness and Residual Harm under the EU AI Act: A Conceptual Framework for Proportional Ex-Ante Controls
explain_beginner: Europe's AI Act sorts AI systems into risk categories, from banned uses down to ones needing almost no oversight, but turning that sorting into real rules that companies can actually follow is not simple. This paper asks how regulators and companies should decide when an AI system's remaining risk, the risk left over after taking safety precautions, is acceptable. Rather than reporting an experiment, the author builds a conceptual framework borrowing ideas from older safety fields like engineering and workplace safety, where a similar question has long been asked. The answer proposed is that companies should be expected to reduce risk until further improvement would be clearly out of proportion to the benefit gained, a standard resembling reasonably achievable safety. It also stresses that a system counts as reasonably safe partly based on how predictable its misuse is and on what current best practice, or the state of the art, allows at the time. The paper concludes this approach makes the law workable, but only if technical standards keep pace with fast-moving AI technology.
explain_business: For a company classifying its AI systems and building a compliance program under the EU AI Act, this paper's practical message is that compliance is not a one-time checklist but an ongoing judgment call, providers of high-risk systems are expected to reduce risk until doing more would be clearly out of proportion to the benefit, not to eliminate risk entirely. That means documenting what was considered reasonably foreseeable misuse, what safeguards were judged proportionate to the risk level, and how the system compares to current state-of-the-art practice, since these three tests are likely to matter in any compliance review or dispute. Following harmonized European standards, once they exist for a given use case, gives a legal presumption of compliance, so tracking which standards apply to a product is a genuinely useful shortcut rather than a formality. The unresolved risk for businesses is that no numeric bar for acceptable residual risk exists yet, so what counts as compliant may keep shifting as EU bodies issue further guidance, meaning compliance programs should be built to adapt.
explain_practitioner: This is a conceptual and legal analysis rather than an empirical study, aiming to operationalize the EU AI Act's four-tier risk model, unacceptable, high-risk, limited-risk, and minimal-risk, by connecting it to established risk-regulation theory. The framework rests on three tests familiar from product safety law, reasonably foreseeable misuse, which asks providers to anticipate predictable user error or integration problems, appropriate measures, which calibrates safeguards to the severity of risk, and state of the art, a technological benchmark that shifts over time. The author argues the Act effectively imports the engineering concept of "as low as reasonably practicable," requiring high-risk AI providers to keep reducing risk until further reduction becomes grossly disproportionate to the benefit gained, and that harmonized standards give providers a presumption of legal compliance once followed. The limitation the author names most directly is that the Act sets no numeric threshold for how much residual risk to fundamental rights is acceptable, leaving that judgment to evolving standards bodies and regulators, which introduces normative ambiguity that only active governance, particularly by the European AI Office, can resolve over time.
